title: Q4 QQQ Roadmap: Navigating AI Turbulence & Market Headwinds
detail:
Q4 QQQ Roadmap: Navigating AI Turbulence & Market Headwinds
Andrew Rocco
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 10:08 AM MST 7 min read
^NDX
CL=F

Let's look at what's actually happening with the Nasdaq 100 (QQQ) as we wrap up 2026.

If you step back and look at the big picture, three clear takeaways stand out:

1) The market is still climbing a massive wall of worry. If someone had told you earlier this year where oil prices and interest rates would end up, you probably wouldn't have believed the market could hold up this well. 

2) AI is carrying the entire narrative. Right now, the economy and the stock market are practically glued to AI. The moment investors worry that data center or infrastructure spending might slow down, tech stocks take an immediate hit.

3) The broad indices don't tell the full story. Serious rotation is happening under the hood. 

From Market Savior to "Tech Destruction" 

Remember last year when everyone complained that big tech was single-handedly dragging the rest of the market up? The script has flipped. QQQ just logged its worst three-day drop since "Liberation Day." In fact, Morgan Stanley noted that U.S. tech momentum recently hit levels worse than during the dot-com bust.

So, what's holding equities back right now? It boils down to four main worries:

• Inflation and stubborn interest rates

• Political headwinds surrounding AI

• Debt and funding fears in AI infrastructure

• Pure technical gravity and profit-taking

Here is why there's good reason to believe the market will push past these hurdles in the coming months.

Inflation & Interest Rates

Recent energy spikes reignited inflation fears and pushed yields higher, but geopolitical energy shocks are usually short-lived. We've already seen oil cool off following reports of potential progress on a U.S.–Iran agreement.

On the rate front, market projections lean toward 3 to 4 quarter-point hikes extending into mid-to-late 2027. But as the team at BlueKurtic Market Insights pointed out, stocks can actually perform quite well during rate-hiking cycles—provided the pace is steady.

This looks more like a limited, non-cyclical adjustment (likely capping out at 2 to 3 hikes) rather than an aggressive tightening regime. The last time we saw a similar non-cyclical adjustment was in 1997, and the S&P 500 went on to gain 40% over the following year.

Politics & the Midterm Effect: Why Gridlock is Good

AI buildouts have run into public pushback—a recent Reuters poll showed only about a third of Americans approve of the current rapid pace of data-center construction. Markets have also been trying to price in the political "Blue Wave," which added fuel to the tech sell-off over fears of tighter regulation.

However, markets are forward-looking mechanisms. This setup is shaping up to be a classic "sell the rumor, buy the news" event.

Historically, a divided government is actually great for stocks—divided setups typically deliver higher average returns than when one party controls both Congress and the White House. On top of that, midterm seasonality is heavily on our side: the S&P 500 has finished higher six months after every single midterm election since 1950. That's 19 straight elections with an average gain of nearly 15%, regardless of who won.

AI Debt & Funding Fears

Fears spiked in October when CoreWeave (CRWV) saw its bond yields jump to distressed levels, causing its stock to tumble. The market briefly priced CRWV as if bankruptcy were imminent—at one point in September, Polymarket showed a 50% chance of a 2027 bankruptcy.

Today? That probability has plummeted to just 12%. The extreme solvency fears were largely overblown.

Technical Gravity & Necessary Reset 

Earlier this year, several AI stocks simply went too far, too fast.

Take SanDisk (SNDK): it blew way past its Fibonacci extensions, surged 4,000% in a single year, and stretched 264% above its 200-day moving average. Anything more than 200% above that trendline is extreme. Think of the 200-day moving average as a rubber band—stretch it too far, and it inevitably snaps back.

Even the strongest market leaders need to reset. What we're seeing right now across names like Marvell (MRVL), Arm Holdings (ARM), and Micron (MU) is a standard pullback to test those major moving averages. Historically, that first test of a rising 200-day line offers one of the best risk-reward entry points you can ask for. 

Bottom Line 

While scary headlines around AI leverage, rates, and politics caused a sharp pull-back, the underlying technical frame of this market remains healthy. Extended tech leaders are flushing out excess leverage and returning to key support levels. Combined with favorable post-midterm seasonality and the benefits of political gridlock, this reset looks less like the end of the run and more like a setup for the next leg higher.

One of the market's strongest trends is the tech sector's resurgence. It's no surprise that the rapid expansion of Artificial Intelligence is driving much of the sector's momentum.

Cloudflare (NET) surged 15% after hours on a blowout quarter, with revenue up 39% and Q4 guidance far above Wall Street's consensus.

While the Nasdaq 100 tracker QQQ fell about 10% in a week, Cloudflare dropped 21%, even before its earnings rebound.

Gross margin slipped to 71% from 74% as Workers carries lower margins, and a $79 billion valuation leaves little room for error.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Cloudflare (NYSE:NET) fell on November 5, 2026, along with the rest of tech. It slid as much as 10% intraday to $238.71, then closed at $244.51. That evening, co-founder and CEO Matthew Prince opened the earnings call by saying, "By nearly every metric, we had our best quarter ever."

24/7 Wall St.

The selloff went well beyond Cloudflare. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), the ETF that tracks the Nasdaq 100, closed at $647.05, down 9.55% over one week. Over the same week, Cloudflare fell 21.2%.

After the report, the stock rose 14.72% after hours to $280.51 as of 7:59 p.m. ET. By our calculation, that still leaves it about 24% below its 52-week high of $370.35.

Shareholders now face a question. Does a beat and raise this large support a $78.93 billion market value while investors are selling high-growth software?

NET Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
What Cloudflare Reported and What It Only Forecast

Revenue was $782.5 million, up 39%. Analysts had expected $736.8 million, and the company's own August guidance was $736 million to $737 million. Non-GAAP EPS came in at $0.38, against a $0.34 estimate.

Non-GAAP operating income reached $137.1 million, a 17.5% margin. Under GAAP accounting, however, Cloudflare still lost $67.9 million from operations and $34.1 million net, or $0.10 a share.

Stock futures are mixed after the major indexes plunged Thursday; futures tied to the Nasdaq 100 were recently up more than 1%, while those associated with the Dow were down nearly 1%; some AI-related stocks that dropped yesterday are among this morning's biggest gainers; new jobs numbers landed, with more hiring than expected last month; bearish attitudes towards AI could affect Anthropic's planned IPO; and Moderna shares are climbing as investors cheered its results and outlook.

Here's what you need to know today.

Stock Futures Mixed After Bruising Thursday Session

Stock futures point to a mixed opening—and a potential shift in momentum after yesterday's big retreat. Futures tied to the Nasdaq 100 were up about 1.4% after the tech-heavy index entered correction territory on Thursday. Futures tied to the S&P 500 were up about 0.2% the morning after it dropped 4.4%. The Dow appeared poised to extend yesterday's losses, with futures tied to the blue-chip index down some 0.9%.

Bitcoin prices slumped more than 5% over the past 24 hours, with the digital currency recently trading around $76,000. Precious metals, including gold, were falling, with a troy ounce of gold selling for about $4,081. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield ticked up slightly to 4.86%. Oil prices were also rising: West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was up about 0.6% to about $90.06 a barrel, while Brent crude, the global benchmark, was up 0.4% to $98.66.

Read Investopedia's full coverage of today's trading here.

Will Tech Stocks Bounce Today?

AI-related stocks that were among the market's worst performers on Thursday may manage to recover today. Data center company Iren (IREN) was among the top premarket climbers, jumping more than 15%. SanDisk (SNDK) was recently up more than 10% while Western Digital (WDC), Micron Technology (MU), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Seagate Technology (STX) were also rising. The Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) was recently up almost 7%, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was up more than 5%.

Elon Musk's two public companies were also rising, with SpaceX (SPCX) up about 5% and Tesla (TSLA) nearly 2%. Musk in an early morning tweet reaffirmed his commitment to Tesla's evolution, saying it would wind down Cybertruck production next year to open factory space for Cybercabs.

Tech sector sentiment is also getting a boost from strong results posted by Cloudflare (NET), another AI investor favorite. Shares of the networking and security services provider, which reported after yesterday's closing bell, were up nearly 20% in premarket trading. Shares of Airbnb (ABNB) jumped 14% after the short-term property rental marketplace boosted its guidance.

The cost of competing in prediction markets is hitting DraftKings (NASDAQ:DKNG) hard after its third-quarter report and first 2027 forecast both fell short of Wall Street's hopes. DraftKings stock is trading at $17.13, down 27%. That decline adds to a steep slide in extended trading after the company released its results following the close on November 5.

Scott Eisen / Getty Images for DraftKings
DKNG Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

This selloff leaves DraftKings stock down 50% year to date. Tech is rallying after a strong October jobs report showed 165,000 jobs added, with the NASDAQ 100 up 2% while the Dow Jones Industrial Average is down 0.6%, so DraftKings is moving on its own news. The company is spending heavily on DraftKings Predictions, its event-contract product supervise by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, as it competes with Kalshi and Polymarket.

DraftKings' 2027 Forecast Falls Short as Predictions Costs Mount

DraftKings guided 2027 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) to a range of $800 million to $1 billion. Analysts surveyed by Bloomberg had expected an average of $1.12 billion. On the top line, DraftKings cut its fiscal 2026 revenue range to $6.35 billion to $6.55 billion, from $6.5 billion to $6.9 billion.

For 2026, DraftKings now sees adjusted EBITDA of $175 million to $275 million, down from $700 million to $900 million. Most of that reduction, DraftKings explained, reflects increased adjusted EBITDA investment in predictions of $650 million to $700 million.

Trend: Price is -20% over 1 month and about 20.7% below the Oct 6 high of $243.37. It sits below every daily moving average. The daily 20 EMA is 209.36, the 50 SMA is 219.93 and the 200 SMA is 204.70. The daily gauge reads Strong Sell.

Broken support: The 200-day SMA at about 204.70 gave way on Nov 5. It is now the first overhead barrier.

Momentum: Daily RSI hit 25.4 on Thursday, the deepest oversold reading in this window, and is now 36.6. Stochastics are oversold (K ≈ 10). That favors a relief bounce, not a trend change.

Trend strength: ADX is 28.9 with -DI at 42.3 against +DI at 10.1, so sellers still control the trend.

Volume: Thursday's volume was 306M shares against a typical 90–150M. That looks like capitulation, but the bounce has to hold on calmer volume.

Weekly view: The weekly summary is Sell. The weekly 100 SMA is about 174.84, and the weekly 50 SMA is about 200.25.

Levels

Resistance: The 193–194 area is the gap-fill zone. Above it sit the Nov 4 close near 200, then the 200-day SMA at ~204.70 and the 20 EMA at ~209. The broken 50 SMA is near 220.

Support: The Thursday low is 181.46. Below it is the July low area around 190, which has already been lost. The classical daily S2/S3 pivots are at 171.83 and 162.10. The 52-week low is 164.27.
